implementation_notes: Foundation's Predicate<Input> (macOS 14 / iOS 17) is the pattern lifted into a first-party type: the #Predicate<T> { ... } macro expands a closure into an expression tree (PredicateExpressions), evaluate(_:) runs it, and the documented operator set inside a predicate body is Boolean logic &&/||/! over comparisons, ranges, optionals and sequence operations - so divide is conjunction and negation is !, while Predicate(all:)/Predicate(any:) fold a collection of predicates (Foundation Preview 6.4+). The payload is the expression tree rather than a closure, which is what framework consumers need: SwiftData queries and Foundation's throwing Sequence.filter(_:) take Predicate values. Prefer plain closures when a rule only ever runs in-process.
pitfalls: #Predicate bodies are expression trees, not executed code: nested declarations, for loops and mutation of captured variables are rejected, and captured values must be constants the framework can encode.
Predicate is @available(macOS 14, iOS 17, tvOS 17, watchOS 10): a framework supporting older platforms needs an availability guard and a closure fallback.
Predicates can be archived and decoded across processes, so unsupported calls or custom types surface as runtime decoding errors that a configuration mistake can easily produce.

variants.name: Plain closures with hand-written combinators
variants.idiom_name: (T) -> Bool closures plus higher-order and/or/not helpers
variants.implementation_notes: Before Predicate (or when a rule must run on older platforms) the carrier is a plain closure (T) -> Bool or (T) -> Result<T, E>, and composition is a higher-order function such as func and<T>(_ a: @escaping (T) -> Bool, _ b: @escaping (T) -> Bool) -> (T) -> Bool { { a($0) && b($0) } }, with switch over an exhaustive enum for choose. The accumulating verdict is your own failure list, and because closures are values they can be stored in arrays and folded. Choose it for in-process validation where the expression-tree machinery and its platform floor add nothing.
pitfalls: An escaping closure stored on the same object it captures creates a retain cycle: capture the fields the rule needs instead of self, and keep rule sets in value types.

Closures are neither comparable nor archivable, so a rule set cannot be diffed, cached or sent across processes - model configuration-driven rules as enums/data and keep closures for code-owned rules.
